disease_name: Acute symptomatic hypernatremia / 急性症候性高ナトリウム血症
disease_name_ja: 急性症候性高ナトリウム血症

distillation_scope.disease_name_only_prompt: Acute symptomatic hypernatremia / 急性症候性高ナトリウム血症 (id: D-ACUTE-SYMPTOMATIC-HYPERNATREMIA)
distillation_scope.leaf_granularity: First-layer metabolic emergency leaf for acute or rapidly progressive hypertonic hypernatremia with neurologic or systemic symptoms. Etiology, chronicity uncertainty, diabetes insipidus, osmotic diuresis, sodium loading, impaired access to water, fever, diarrhea, burns, renal failure, or treatment response are represented as mechanisms, axes, risk modifiers, or treatment modifiers rather than disease-name qualifiers.
distillation_scope.boundary_policy: This manifold describes the acute physiologic state of symptomatic extracellular sodium and effective tonicity excess. Central diabetes insipidus, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, hyperglycemic osmotic diuresis, heat illness, gastroenteritis, renal failure, or iatrogenic sodium loading can be driver contexts or separate comorbid manifolds, not appended to the disease_id.
distillation_scope.case_separation_note: No real case evidence was searched, read, or structured for this disease distillation.

latent_mechanisms.display_name_ja: 高張性ナトリウム・水バランス異常
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Integrated burden of extracellular sodium and effective tonicity excess from free-water deficit, hypotonic water loss, or hypertonic sodium gain.

latent_mechanisms.display_name_ja: 口渇反応または飲水アクセス障害
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Reduced ability to sense thirst, communicate need, or obtain water; makes any ongoing water loss clinically dangerous.
Central or nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, osmotic diuresis, post-obstructive diuresis, loop diuretics, or recovery from AKI cause urine water loss that exceeds intake.
Fever, heat exposure, sweating, burns, tachypnea, diarrhea, vomiting, fistula output, or inadequate replacement of insensible losses remove water in excess of sodium.

latent_mechanisms.display_name_ja: 高張性ナトリウム負荷
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Iatrogenic or ingested sodium load from hypertonic saline, sodium bicarbonate, salt poisoning, hypertonic dialysis or feeds, or excess sodium replacement raises extracellular tonicity directly.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Brain cell shrinkage and vascular stretch injury
latent_mechanisms.display_name_ja: 脳細胞脱水と血管伸展障害
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Rapid extracellular hypertonicity pulls water out of brain cells before organic osmolyte adaptation, causing irritability, lethargy, confusion, seizure, coma, subdural or intracerebral bleeding risk, and severe encephalopathy.

latent_mechanisms.display_name_ja: 低容量性低灌流と腎障害
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Water loss commonly contracts extracellular volume, raising BUN/creatinine and producing tachycardia, hypotension, shock, AKI, and reduced reserve for sodium correction.

latent_mechanisms.display_name_ja: 制御された自由水補正と原因制御
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Enteral water, intravenous electrolyte-free water, volume stabilization, DI control, osmotic diuresis control, and sodium-load removal lower sodium and tonicity at a neurologically safe rate.

latent_mechanisms.display_name_ja: 過急補正による脳浮腫
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Rapid fall in sodium after brain osmolyte adaptation can move water into brain cells, causing headache, vomiting, seizure, worsening mental status, cerebral edema, or herniation physiology.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Thirst or water-access failure allows hypertonicity to emerge from otherwise compensated water losses.
Electrolyte-free urine water loss raises sodium when intake cannot keep up.
Insensible, GI, skin, or respiratory water loss concentrates extracellular sodium.
Sodium gain raises extracellular sodium and effective tonicity directly.
Serum sodium is the core measured expression of hypernatremia.
Corrected sodium preserves the hypertonic sodium signal when hyperglycemia shifts water extracellularly.
Hypernatremia raises measured serum osmolality unless offset by unusual measurement context.
Effective tonicity drives cellular water movement and neurologic injury.
A rapidly rising sodium marks acute hypernatremic stress and limited cerebral adaptation.
Acute onset separates rapid osmotic injury from chronic adaptation risk.
Renal water loss commonly presents with polyuria.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: may fall when severe hypovolemia or AKI supervenes
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: DI and osmotic diuresis increase urine volume before shock or AKI limits output.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: low in diabetes insipidus, high in osmotic diuresis
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Urine osmolality distinguishes water diuresis from osmotic diuresis without forcing an etiology label.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: low in diabetes insipidus, higher in osmotic diuresis
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Specific gravity is a bedside correlate of urine concentration.
Central DI is a renal free-water-loss context when AVP is deficient.
Renal AVP resistance produces free-water loss and blunts desmopressin response.
Glucose, mannitol, urea, post-obstructive solute, or high-protein tube feeds can drive osmotic urine water loss.
GI, skin, respiratory, or fever-related water loss can be visible in history and exam.
Hypertonic sodium intake or infusion is the structured exposure context for sodium-gain hypernatremia.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: more likely when sodium gain exceeds renal excretion or when kidney reserve is poor
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Sodium loading can pair hypernatremia with extracellular volume expansion.
Observed inability to drink, dementia, delirium, intubation, immobility, or lack of water access supports this mechanism.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: thirst may be intense if intact and absent/blunted if impaired
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: A missing thirst response despite hypertonicity is a major clue to impaired water-intake physiology.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: strongest when sodium rises rapidly or absolute sodium is very high
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Extracellular hypertonicity dehydrates brain cells and stretches bridging vessels.
Hypernatremic encephalopathy produces irritability, confusion, lethargy, obtundation, or coma.
Neurologic severity tracks acute tonicity burden and brain dehydration.
Lethargy is a specific satellite phenotype of hypernatremic encephalopathy.
Somnolence can occur with severe hypertonic encephalopathy and stays gated by the mental-status parent.
Seizure can occur in severe acute hypernatremia or during cerebral edema from treatment.
Vascular stretch injury or intracranial bleeding can produce focal deficits.
Brain dehydration is the immediate life-threatening neurologic pathway.
Brain shrinkage can tear bridging veins or injure cerebral vessels, especially in infants and older adults.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: strongest when water loss rather than sodium gain dominates
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Most hypernatremia is water-deficit physiology with extracellular volume contraction.
Clinical dehydration is a visible expression of water deficit.
Extracellular volume contraction accompanies hypotonic water loss when sodium loss or poor intake coexists.
Prerenal azotemia and dehydration raise BUN.
Hypoperfusion or underlying renal disease raises creatinine and limits water/sodium handling.
Severe volume contraction can produce shock.
Prerenal hypoperfusion and hypertonic stress can transition into AKI.
Treatment-related cerebral edema can present with seizure.
Severe encephalopathy is a major near-term death pathway.
Shock and poor perfusion directly increase death hazard.
Intracranial bleeding adds direct neurologic mortality risk.
Severe correction-related cerebral edema can cause herniation or fatal neurologic decline.

Measured and effective osmolality usually move together, but urea and glucose context can separate them.
Rapid rise leaves less time for brain adaptation.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Prerenal urea retention accompanies water deficit.
Hemodynamic volume deficit is the immediate shock pathway.
Renal hypoperfusion can transition to AKI.

treatments.display_name: Enteral water or intravenous dextrose water replacement
treatments.display_name_ja: 経口・経腸水分または5%ブドウ糖液による自由水補充

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Excessively fast sodium lowering can create cerebral edema, especially if chronicity is not truly acute.
Acute sodium gain or rapid water loss has less brain osmolyte adaptation, so neurologic rescue can require faster early lowering.
Heart failure, renal failure, or sodium-load states can make free-water volume difficult to deliver safely.

side_effects.interpretation: Risk rises when sodium is lowered too quickly for brain adaptation.
Large free-water volumes can overload vulnerable patients.

treatments.context_specific_role: Directly treats hypertonicity and water deficit; rate must be controlled by measured sodium trajectory and ongoing losses.

treatments.display_name: Isotonic crystalloid resuscitation for hypovolemic shock
treatments.display_name_ja: 低容量性ショックに対する等張晶質液蘇生

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Isotonic resuscitation is for perfusion rescue, not isolated free-water deficit.
Fluid tolerance can be low in heart failure, kidney failure, or sodium-gain states.

side_effects.interpretation: Isotonic fluid may not lower sodium and can delay free-water correction if used beyond perfusion need.

treatments.context_specific_role: Stabilizes perfusion first when shock is present; free-water correction then addresses tonicity.

treatments.display_name: Desmopressin for central DI or excess water diuresis
treatments.display_name_ja: 中枢性尿崩症または過剰水利尿に対するデスモプレシン

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: AVP deficiency should respond with lower urine output and higher urine osmolality.
Renal AVP resistance blunts desmopressin effect.
Desmopressin plus free water can rapidly lower sodium if not monitored.

side_effects.interpretation: Antidiuresis can accelerate sodium lowering when free water is being given.

treatments.context_specific_role: Controls ongoing renal water loss when central DI or uncontrolled aquaresis is active.

treatments.display_name_ja: 腎性尿崩症ドライバー管理

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Lithium exposure, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia, or chronic tubulointerstitial disease makes renal water-loss control relevant.
Thiazide-like antidiuresis strategies require careful volume and electrolyte monitoring.

side_effects.interpretation: Diuretic-based nephrogenic DI strategies can worsen volume status if mismatched.

treatments.context_specific_role: Longer-horizon reduction of renal free-water loss when AVP resistance is active; not an immediate substitute for water replacement.

treatments.display_name_ja: 浸透圧利尿・高血糖の制御

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Hyperglycemia or other osmoles sustain renal water loss until controlled.
Corrected sodium may rise during glucose lowering even as measured sodium changes.

treatments.context_specific_role: Reduces ongoing osmotic urine water loss and clarifies corrected sodium trajectory.

treatments.display_name: Stop hypertonic sodium or excess solute load
treatments.display_name_ja: 高張性ナトリウム・過剰溶質負荷の中止

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Removing sodium input only helps when sodium loading is active.
Enteral solute load often persists unless feed concentration and water flushes are corrected.

treatments.context_specific_role: Removes ongoing sodium or solute pressure so water replacement is not immediately counteracted.

treatments.display_name: Loop diuretic plus free water for sodium or volume overload
treatments.display_name_ja: ナトリウム・容量過剰に対するループ利尿薬と自由水補充

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Diuresis cannot remove sodium effectively without urine output.
Diuresis is dangerous when the dominant problem is water deficit and shock.

side_effects.interpretation: Overdiuresis can worsen hypovolemia and sodium concentration.

treatments.context_specific_role: Useful when sodium overload or volume overload makes pure free-water delivery unsafe and renal output is preserved.

treatments.display_name: Renal replacement therapy for refractory sodium overload or renal failure
treatments.display_name_ja: 難治性ナトリウム過剰・腎不全に対する腎代替療法

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: RRT is most relevant when renal failure, sodium overload, or fluid intolerance prevents safe conventional correction.
Dialysate or replacement fluid sodium must be matched to avoid abrupt tonicity shifts.

side_effects.interpretation: Too-low dialysate sodium or fast clearance can overcorrect.

treatments.context_specific_role: Extracorporeal control of sodium and water when kidneys or fluid tolerance cannot safely achieve correction.

treatments.display_name_ja: 気道保護とけいれん対応

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Lower GCS increases airway protection value.
Active seizure adds hypoxia, aspiration, and metabolic demand risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Prevents secondary hypoxic injury while sodium and water correction addresses the primary osmotic driver.

present.trajectory_modulation: Adds high-solute urine losses and makes corrected sodium more informative than measured sodium alone.

treatment_effect_modulation.osmotic_diuresis_and_hyperglycemia_contr: stronger when solute diuresis remains active

present.trajectory_modulation: Increases ongoing free-water needs and strengthens dehydration/volume-depletion geometry.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Observed GI, skin, or heat loss is direct driver evidence.

present.trajectory_modulation: Supports rapid sodium-gain physiology and can pair hypernatremia with volume overload rather than dehydration.

treatment_effect_modulation.loop_diuretic_plus_free_water_for_sodium: more relevant when sodium load coexists with volume overload

present.trajectory_modulation: Constrains endogenous sodium/water handling and narrows safe treatment path.

Extracorporeal control may be needed when kidneys cannot regulate sodium and water.

treatment_effect_modulation.renal_replacement_therapy_for_refractory: stronger when renal failure or fluid intolerance is active
treatment_effect_modulation.enteral_water_or_intravenous_dextrose_wa: requires closer volume and sodium monitoring

present.trajectory_modulation: Does not cause acute symptomatic hypernatremia but raises treatment toxicity if sodium is lowered as though the disorder were definitely acute.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Adapted brain is vulnerable to rapid lowering.
Unknown or chronic cases require stricter correction-rate control.

supportive_care: Track serum sodium, glucose-corrected sodium, effective tonicity, urine output, urine osmolality, volume status, and mental status together; serum sodium alone is not enough.
Do not encode central DI, nephrogenic DI, osmotic diuresis, hypertonic saline exposure, or impaired access to water in the disease_id; they are context axes or treatment modifiers.

Preserve parent/satellite structure for symptoms and findings: thirst, dehydration, renal water loss, extrarenal water loss, mental status, seizure, focal neurologic deficit, nausea, vomiting, and generalized weakness.
Correction rate is a state variable and treatment-toxicity mediator, not a hand-written treatment ranking label.
When shock is present, perfusion rescue and tonicity correction are separate vector-field effects; isotonic crystalloid fixes perfusion but does not substitute for free-water replacement.
New seizure, worsening headache, vomiting, or mental-status decline during correction should raise cerebral-edema-from-correction hazard rather than being deleted as contradictory evidence.
In hyperglycemic or osmotic diuresis contexts, corrected sodium and ongoing urinary losses determine the trajectory; measured sodium can move unexpectedly during glucose correction.
No real case evidence was used to shape this distillation.
